= Module 02: Hands-on Exercise
:navtitle: Module 02: Hands-on Exercise

In this module you will follow a metered MaaS request through the gateway end to end and
observe the quota enforcement layer that external metering works alongside.

**Learning objectives:**

* Trace a request through the pre-inference credit check and the post-inference usage webhook
* Identify the fields in the emitted token usage event
* Inspect the gateway authentication and rate limit policies generated by the MaaS controller

== Exercise 1: Follow a metered request

Walk through the lifecycle of a single inference request on a metered gateway:

. A user sends an inference request to a MaaS-published model through the API gateway.
. The pre-inference credit check plugin asks the external metering system whether the
requester still has credit. If credit is exhausted, the request is blocked and no model
compute is spent on it.
. The model processes the request.
. The post-inference token usage webhook plugin asynchronously emits a structured token
usage event to the configured external metering endpoint.

The emitted event carries the following fields:

|===
|Field |Description

|Requester identity
|The user who made the inference request

|Subscription
|The MaaS subscription the requester belongs to

|Model
|The MaaS-published model that served the request

|Input and output token counts
|Token usage recorded for the request

|Request ID
|Identifier for correlating the event with the original request

|Timestamp
|When the request completed

|===

TIP: The webhook delivers asynchronously, so metering does not add latency to the inference
path. The credit check also keeps metering latency out of the request path: when credit is
exhausted, only the next request is blocked rather than every in-flight request waiting on
the metering system.

== Exercise 2: Observe the quota enforcement layer

The MaaS controller generates gateway authentication and rate limit policies for each
published model, and the external metering plugins run alongside this quota layer. List
the MaaSModelRef resources to find the project namespace of each published model, then
list the generated policies in that namespace:

[source,bash,role="execute",subs="attributes"]
----
oc get maasmodelref --all-namespaces
oc get authpolicy -n <model_namespace>
oc get tokenratelimitpolicy -n <model_namespace>
----

where `<model_namespace>` is the project namespace where the model is deployed. Each
published model should have a corresponding AuthPolicy and TokenRateLimitPolicy
created by the controller. If these policies are missing, check the MaaS controller logs
for errors.

=== Verify

Note what you observe against the documented behavior:

* Blocked requests when credit is exhausted — the pre-inference credit check blocks the
next request once credit runs out.
* Failed webhook delivery attempts are logged for alerting and recovery, so operators can
detect a metering endpoint that has stopped accepting events.

IMPORTANT: The integration emits raw usage events only. Invoice generation, cost
attribution, and rate calculation are the responsibility of the external metering system,
so the numbers you see in your billing system are produced there, not in OpenShift AI.

== Module summary

**What you accomplished:**

* Traced a metered request through the credit check, inference, and usage webhook stages
* Identified every field in the emitted token usage event
* Inspected the AuthPolicy and TokenRateLimitPolicy resources the MaaS controller generates

**Key takeaways:**

* The credit check runs before inference and blocks only when credit is exhausted
* Usage events flow asynchronously after each request and include requester, subscription, model, token counts, request ID, and timestamp
* External metering provides raw event emission; billing math lives in the external system

**Next steps:**

Continue to the conclusion, where you review what you covered and find the product
documentation for external metering and MaaS governance.
